title: TENORMIN (atenolol) tablets: prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling (NDA018240), published in DailyMed; structured product labelling version 2, published 1 May 2026, label information updated 18 September 2025
funder: not stated; FDA-approved labelling carries no funding statement. The labeller submits the text and the Food and Drug Administration approves it.
result: A beta1-selective blocker without membrane-stabilising or intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; selectivity is not absolute and higher doses inhibit beta2 adrenoceptors in bronchial and vascular muscle. About 50% of an oral dose is absorbed, it undergoes little or no hepatic metabolism and is eliminated mainly by the kidney, half-life about 6 to 7 hours, with significant accumulation below a creatinine clearance of 35 ml/min/1.73 m2; elderly patients have about 50% lower clearance. No boxed warning. Warnings: beta blockade can depress myocardial contractility and precipitate cardiac failure, including in patients without previous failure; severe exacerbation of angina, myocardial infarction and ventricular arrhythmias after abrupt discontinuation in angina, possibly without preceding angina, so abrupt cessation is avoided even in hypertension; bradycardia and heart block with verapamil or diltiazem; bronchospastic disease; masking of hypoglycaemia and risk of severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially in diabetes, children and fasting patients; masking of hyperthyroidism and possible thyroid storm on withdrawal; untreated phaeochromocytoma; fetal harm: atenolol from the second trimester has been associated with infants small for gestational age, and neonates exposed at parturition or through breastfeeding may develop hypoglycaemia and bradycardia; peripheral arterial circulatory disorders may be aggravated; patients with previous anaphylaxis may react more severely and be unresponsive to usual adrenaline doses. In controlled hypertension studies with elicited reports (399 on atenolol, 407 on placebo): tiredness 26% against 13%, cold extremities 12% against 5%, dizziness 13% against 6%, depression 12% against 9%, dreaming 3% against 1%, dyspnoea 6% against 4%. Postmarketing reports include impotence, Peyronie's disease, psychoses, hallucinations, exacerbation of psoriasis, antinuclear antibodies, lupus syndrome and Raynaud's phenomenon. In ISIS-1 (16,027 patients with suspected infarction), vascular mortality in days 0 to 7 was 3.89% (313 deaths) on atenolol against 4.57% (365), and dosing was reduced or stopped for cardiogenic shock in 4 intravenous and 35 oral cases and for heart block above first degree in 5 and 143.
